papers.title: Sexual competition can select for male-only semelparity
papers.abstract: Semelparity, - reproducing once in a lifetime - is an extreme solution to the trade-off between reproduction and future survival and is exceedingly rare in terrestrial vertebrates. Males of the Australian genera Antechinus, Phascogale and Dasykaluta are obligately semelparous while females are iteroparous, suggesting that the sexes face such different selective pressures that they have evolved different solutions to the same trade-off. Using invasion analyses of a novel two-sex population model with continuous reproductive investment, we show that the geometry of the reproduction-survival trade-off determines whether semelparity is evolutionarily accessible, but not necessarily whether it evolves. Age-structured survival and fecundity may maintain iteroparity under trade-off shapes for which classical theory predicts semelparity. Early onset of post-reproductive mortality can flip otherwise iteroparous trade-offs to semelparity, but only when survival declines quickly after sexual maturity. In contrast, when sexual competition gives high-investing males sufficiently disproportionate paternity, male-only semelparity can evolve under any trade-off geometry we examined, while females remain iteroparous. That male-only semelparity is rare while male competition is common suggests that lethal male investment evolves only under a particular combination of demographic, environmental and mating-system conditions.

papers.title: Precision Fermentation Gets a New Player: Genome Assembly and Genetic Transformation of a Novel Strain, Pichia hangzhouana, for Precision Fermentation of Food Ingredients
papers.abstract: Precision fermentation leverages the metabolic pathways of microorganisms to produce valuable proteins and enzymes. Pichia hangzhouana, synonymous with Zygoascus hellenicus, is a non-conventional yeast with potential for food biotechnological applications. This study characterizes the CSIRO strain P. hangzhouana FRR5246, isolated from a tea beverage, to evaluate its suitability as a precision fermentation host for a variety of industrial, agricultural and food production applications. P. hangzhouana demonstrated robust growth across a range of carbon sources, with the highest optical density observed in media containing sucrose or sorbitol as sole carbon source. The yeast showed susceptibility to geneticin, hygromycin B, nourseothricin sulfate, and zeocin sulfate antibiotic agents. Successful genetic transformation was achieved, with the expression of a recombinant orange fluorescent protein (OFP) under the control of the native glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAP1) promoter. The secretome exhibited strong antimicrobial activity against Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus, indicating the presence of potent antimicrobial compounds. In addition, whole genome sequencing of P. hangzhouana FRR5246 provided genetic tools for recombinant expression of heterologous genes, insight into the genes, genetic architecture and regulatory mechanisms underlying phenotypic qualities, as well as confirming phylogenetic classification of this strain as clustering with the Dipodascomycetes, most closely related to species Zygoascus hellenicus. P. hangzhouana FRR5246 is a promising candidate for precision fermentation of food ingredients, capable of utilizing diverse carbon sources and producing recombinant proteins. In addition, production of antimicrobial compounds further enhances the potential for biotechnological exploitation. Future work will focus on optimizing growth conditions and exploring native inducible promoters for controlled gene expression.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal Dynamics and Environmental Drivers of Maize Microbiome Structure across Diverse Agroecosystems in Georgia, USA
papers.abstract: The understanding of how microbial communities differ across soils, environments, plant tissues, and developmental stages is key to the improvement of crop productivity and resilience. Here, we conducted a statewide survey of maize (Zea mays L.) microbiomes across 35 fields at 16 locations in Georgia, USA, sampling soil, rhizosphere, root interior, and stalk interior at two developmental stages (600 and 1400 growing degree days, GDD). More than 38000 ASVs were produced after amplicon sequencing of 16S rRNA genes. The phyla shown to be dominant are Proteobacteria, Actinobacteriota, Chloroflexi, Planctomycetota, and Acidobacteriota. Based on alpha and beta diversity analyses, the below-ground compartments (soil and rhizosphere) revealed higher diversity and stronger spatial structuring when compared to the above-ground sample types, whereas root and stalk interior microbiomes revealed marked shifts across growth stages. Amino acid metabolism, secondary metabolite biosynthesis, and energy-related pathways predictions (via PICRUSt2) show stage-dependent enrichment. Network analyses show persistent keystone taxa (Proteobacteria and Actinobacteriota) mediating microbial stability, coupled with an increase in modularity and connectivity as we move from early to late growth stages. Some environmental variables, such as temperature, humidity, soil potassium, and soil sodium, showed significant correlation with microbial diversity indicative of a compartment-specific environmental sensitivity. Collectively, our results show that in maize, microbial community composition, interaction, and potential functionality are both impacted by developmental stages and environmental heterogeneity. This study provides a fundamental framework for understanding the microbiome dynamics in field-grown maize across various agroecological conditions. It equally provides ecological insights relevant to microbiome-informed crop management.

papers.title: Gene regulatory networks and the organization of cell differentiation in multicellular organisms
papers.abstract: Across their development, clonal multicellular organisms generate new cell types from less differentiated cell types. Differentiation pathways arrange into a hierarchical, tree-like organization: regressions from specialized to undifferentiated cell types rarely occur and undifferentiated cell types often have the potential to produce, when subject to distinct stimuli, two or more differently specialized cell types. How cell type transitions acquire such a peculiar disposition requires an explanation that must reside in the properties of gene regulatory networks (GRNs); after all, GRNs orchestrate the changes in gene activity that define cell types. We studied vast numbers of small dynamic model networks to search for elementary GRNs that could yield the simplest hierarchical, developmental-like, differentiation patterns. We found that only a small minority of GRNs are compatible with hierarchical cell type transitions. Importantly, GRNs that yielded developmental-like differentiation patterns shared common traits: One is the presence of tangles of cycles of positive interactions. Genes in such a tangle produce an all-or-none one-way response to a signal. Another such trait is mutual inhibition between genes associated to different specialized cell types, enforcing their mutually exclusive activation. Moreover, these regulatory patterns are more abundant in published experimentally sustained developmental GRNs than as expected by chance. In addition, we show that it is easy to maintain hierarchical cellular differentiation throughout evolution, even when undergoing changes in gene regulatory interactions and developmental mechanisms. Our work supports the prevalence of design principles that organize hierarchically differentiation pathways in clonal multicellular organisms.

papers.title: Large-scale 3D stitching montage cryo-electron tomography reveals heterogeneity and connectivity of lamellipodial actin networks
papers.abstract: Cellular processes range from local interactions among a few proteins to micrometer-scale assemblies whose coordinated components give rise to emergent properties. A prime example is the actin cytoskeleton in protrusive structures at the leading edge of migrating cells, termed lamellipodia. Significant progress has been made in understanding the functional contributions of distinct actin-filament populations and associated proteins within lamellipodia. Yet, a detailed quantitative appreciation of how actin filaments form a spatially connected and interdependent network has been impeded by limitations of existing methods. Cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) can visualize such biological entities at molecular resolution in native cellular environments, but its limited field-of -view constrains quantitative analysis of extended assemblies. Hence, how lamellipodial actin architectures collectively support productive migration is not completely understood. Here, we present a 3D stitching montage cryo-ET workflow that advances both methodological and biological frontiers through its application to lamellipodia. We combine large-area montage-tilt series acquisition with independent tile reconstruction, denoising, and optical flow-based three-dimensional stitching to reconstruct large regions of the leading edge up to ~ 100 m2 at single-filament resolution. Bridging molecular resolution and cellular-scale context allows comprehensive filament tracing and quantification of actin filament networks, providing parameters for models of force generation in motile cells. Our data reveal that the network architecture in a seemingly uniform protrusive lamellipodium is markedly heterogeneous. By mapping Arp2/3 branch junction-based connectivity, using the molecular resolution of our data, we show how branch-junction distribution and network connectivity vary as a function of filament density and distance from the leading edge. We also identify the complex coexistence of short, branched and long, unbranched filament assemblies. We provide montage 3D volumes and filament vectorizations through an interactive, open web-based resource for browsing and interrogating the data. Our work thus provides a quantitative reference for lamellipodial actin architecture and a scalable approach for large-scale cryo-ET.

papers.title: Inactive X chromosome DNA methylation erosion with age in human dermal fibroblasts
papers.abstract: X chromosome inactivation is an epigenetic process that establishes dosage compensation between the sexes through the monoallelic silencing of one X chromosome in karyotypically normal females. The allele that becomes inactivated is determined randomly during early development, resulting in females being mosaic with respect to whether the maternal or paternal allele is inactivated. This mosaicism makes it technically challenging to separate the active and inactive chromosomes in bulk populations, and consequently it has been historically difficult to study X chromosome inactivation in human cells. Here we use long read sequencing of 31 single cell clones derived from primary human dermal fibroblasts from 7 donors aged 25-80 years, and generate a method to distinguish DNA methylation state of the active versus the inactive X chromosome. As expected, CpG islands (CGIs) on the inactive X chromosome have high levels of methylation, while CGIs on the active X chromosome are very lowly methylated. Notably, we observe substantial loss of DNA methylation across multiple CGIs on the inactive X chromosome in an age dependent manner. We also observe this DNA methylation erosion in bulk samples by quantifying CGI methylation levels across individual sequencing reads. The genes that show age-related erosion of CGI methylation are associated with increased total transcription suggesting this methylation erosion generates a transcriptional permissive state. Overall, our study provides evidence of erosion of X chromosome inactivation with age in cell lines derived from primary human samples and implicates a role for loss of DNA methylation in the increased dosage of X chromosome linked genes in females with age. These findings shed new light on the epigenetic instability of the inactive X chromosome during human ageing and may be linked to age-related cellular dysfunction in females.

papers.title: Loss of SRF-driven contractility, not lymphatic smooth muscle cell loss, is the primary driver of age-associated collecting vessel decline
papers.abstract: The lymphatic vasculature returns interstitial fluid to the blood circulation, a function that depends on rhythmic contraction of the smooth muscle cells (SMCs) surrounding collecting vessels. Lymph transport declines with age, a decline attributed largely to loss of SMCs from collecting vessels. We show that the principal change is not their loss but the loss of their contractile phenotype. In mouse ear collecting vessels, contractile protein expression declined with age and the vessels dilated, yet the majority of SMCs remained on the vessel wall. The decline extended to serum response factor (SRF), the transcription factor driving the smooth muscle contractile gene programme, and was mirrored by a loss of SRF-dependent contractile transcripts in published single-cell data from aged lymphatic muscle cells. Inducible deletion of Srf in mural cells reproduced this state, abolishing the contractile programme while leaving the cells in place and thereby excluding impaired SMC recruitment as the main mechanism. The resulting vessels became severely dilated and misshapen, whereas lymphatic capillaries were unaffected; endothelial identity, valve formation and lymphatic endothelial cell (LEC) number were all preserved, with enlargement instead reflecting increased LEC size. Intravital imaging showed loss of both rhythmic contraction and the contractile movement of individual SMCs, and Evans blue drainage to the inguinal lymph node was correspondingly reduced. Deletion of Srf after the contractile phenotype was established recapitulated this loss, showing that SRF is required continuously to maintain lymphatic SMC contractility and providing a genetic model of age-associated lymphatic dysfunction.

papers.title: Endogenous activation of multiple stress-response pathways during meiosis promotes gamete fitness
papers.abstract: Gametogenesis, the process of meiosis coupled to gamete formation, transforms diploid progenitor cells into haploid gametes through extensive cellular remodeling and rewiring of gene expression. Several stress-responsive transcription factors (TFs) are upregulated during gametogenesis, but whether the cellular mechanisms that handle environmental stress also support the success of this developmental process is largely unexplored. Here, we show that four stress-responsive TFs, Hsf1, Skn7, and the paralogs Msn2 and Msn4, are endogenously active during budding yeast gametogenesis in the absence of external stress and drive distinct gene expression programs. Simultaneous meiotic depletion of Msn2, Msn4, and Skn7 compromise the fitness of the resulting gametes. We identified just two TF-dependent targets, the antioxidant genes TSA1 and AHP1, as important for gamete fitness, directly connecting TF activity to the protection of meiotic progeny. Our results demonstrate that the activation of canonical stress-response regulators is built into the meiotic program and suggest that such pathways can be repurposed during development to safeguard cellular health.

papers.title: Mutations in core Ccr4-NOT subunits manifest links to decapping rather than deadenylation in Saccharomyces cerevisiae
papers.abstract: The mRNA polyadenosine tail (pA-tail) is gradually shortened in the cytoplasm by two main deadenylase complexes, Ccr4-NOT and Pan2/3, eventually leading to decapping and decay. The yeast Ccr4-NOT complex contains two deadenylases, Ccr4 and Pop2, and seven non-catalytic subunits. The functions of the latter are not yet fully understood. Here, we investigate the role of Ccr4-NOT in RNA metabolism in budding yeast. We show that steady-state mRNA pA-tail lengths increase with growth temperature, with this effect enhanced in ccr4{Delta} and pop2{Delta} cells, indicating a role for Ccr4-NOT in temperature-dependent mRNA regulation. Consistent with a functional divergence between species, we confirm that Ccr4 is the predominant deadenylase in yeast, whereas the Pop2 orthologs CNOT7/8 are the major deadenylases in human cells. Using Illumina and direct RNA sequencing, we characterize yeast strains defective in Ccr4-NOT, Pan2/3, or mRNA decapping. Unexpectedly, we show that loss of NOT1, NOT2, NOT4 or POP2 causes transcriptome and pA-tail changes resembling those of the decapping-factor mutants dhh1{Delta} and lsm1{Delta}, rather than of the principal deadenylase mutant ccr4{Delta}, and induces a mild stress response. Loss of Not2 or Not4 prolongs the half-lives of several mRNAs and causes growth defects comparable to decapping co-factor mutants. The mRNAs stabilized by loss of Not1-2-4 are distinct from those preferentially deadenylated by Ccr4-Pop2, suggesting different substrate targeting by Ccr4-NOT for non-overlapping functions in deadenylation and decapping.

papers.title: Comparative landscape of extracellular vesicles across three pathogenic trematodes identifies a key conserved miRNA cargo involved in host liver fibrosis
papers.abstract: Liver fibrosis caused by Schistosoma japonicum, Clonorchis sinensis, and Opisthorchis felineus represents a major global public health burden. Here, we systematically characterized extracellular vesicles (EVs) released by key stages of these parasites and uncovered, for the first time, a conserved repertoire of EV-derived miRNAs shared across all three species. By integrating animal models, single-cell RNA sequencing, and bioinformatic analyses, we comprehensively identified the targetome of miR-36-3p, a cross-species conserved miRNA cargo. Mechanistically, we found that miR-36-3p directly targets Atox1 in Kupffer cells, driving intracellular copper and reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation and thereby activating hepatic stellate cells. Strikingly, in vivo delivery of an AAV8-encoded miR-36-3p sponge markedly attenuated liver fibrosis across all three infection models. Collectively, these findings establish a conserved, parasite-derived EV miRNA cargo as a previously unrecognized driver of host liver pathology and identify it as a promising therapeutic target for preventing parasite-induced liver fibrosis.

papers.title: A small molecule inhibits Neisseria gonorrhoeae pilus formation
papers.abstract: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is becoming increasingly antimicrobial-resistant. N. gonorrhoeae requires the Type IV pilus (T4p) for pathogenesis, wherein the T4p promotes colonization through adherence to host cells and resistance to neutrophil killing. The pilus also is required for natural transformation and twitching motility. Collectively, these critical functions make the T4p an attractive drug target. Previously, we developed a high-throughput screen to identify compounds with activity against the zinc metalloprotease Mpg, which is involved in T4p biogenesis. Here, we identified a lead compound, SC144, that inhibits Mpg peptidoglycan-hydrolyzing activity in both N. gonorrhoeae and other bacteria encoding Mpg-like M23B metallopeptidase orthologs. Interestingly, SC144 targets Mpgs carboxypeptidase and endopeptidase activities. Importantly, SC144 inhibited N. gonorrhoeae colonization and prevented its survival in two primary human cell culture models of infection without toxic effects on these host cells. This work provides strong evidence that SC144 is a promising lead compound with anti-virulence activity against N. gonorrhoeae.

papers.title: Two novel plant-derived yeast species in Thailandicola (Microbotryomycetes): comparative genomics and transformation
papers.abstract: Plant tissues and surfaces are among the largest microbial habitats on Earth, and commensal yeasts are common members of these communities, where they can contribute to plant-microbe interactions including the biological control of plant diseases. Here, we describe two novel species of unpigmented, basidiomycete yeasts, in the class Microbotryomycetes from the plant phyllosphere (Thailandicola erigeronia and T. cardamina) represented by three isolates from leaves of multiple hosts. We characterize these taxa through analyses of metabolic requirements, tolerance to differences in osmolarity, pH, and temperature, and enzymatic activities. In parallel, we generate near-chromosome-scale hybrid genomes annotated with transcriptome data for these novel species and a congenic isolate. We employ whole-genome and multilocus phylogenetic approaches to infer the placement of these species within a monophyletic clade. We use comparative genomics to examine how the gene content of these yeasts differs from that of other members of the Microbotryomycetes, including an apparent proliferation of retrotransposons. We further demonstrate the genetic transformability of these taxa using Agrobacterium tumefaciens-mediated transformation. The description of these new species, together with high-quality genome resources and a genetic transformation protocol, establishes a foundation for experimental studies of these novel plant-derived yeasts and their interactions with hosts and other microbes.

papers.title: PRC2-mediated H3K27me3 uncouples PHE1 binding from transcriptional activation at imprinted genes
papers.abstract: Genomic imprinting results in parent-of-origin-dependent gene expression and plays an important role in endosperm development. The type I MADS-box transcription factor PHERES1 (PHE1) has been implicated in the regulation of imprinted genes, particularly paternally expressed genes (PEGs). Silencing of the maternal alleles of PEGs is mediated by repressive histone modifications, including H3K27me3 established by the Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2). Here, we established an adapted low-input CUT&Tag protocol to profile the allele-specific genome-wide binding of PHE1 in the endosperm and compared the resulting binding profiles with previously published ChIP-seq data. Our CUT&Tag analysis substantially recapitulated the previously identified PHE1-binding landscape while requiring considerably less input material. Consistent with earlier findings, PHE1 binding was enriched at RC/Helitron transposable elements and imprinted genes, specifically PEGs. Interestingly, most PHE1-bound PEGs exhibited binding on both maternal and paternal alleles despite H3K27me3 enrichment on their maternal alleles. Perturbation of H3K27me3 deposition did not alter the predominantly biallelic PHE1 occupancy observed at these loci, supporting that PHE1 binding can persist in an H3K27me3-associated chromatin environment. In contrast, analysis of gene expression in fertilization independent seed (fis) prc2 mutants impaired in H3K27me3 establishment caused increased expression of PHE1 targets and altered their parent-of-origin-specific expression patterns. Our findings reveal that biallelic transcription factor occupancy can coexist with parent-of-origin-specific transcriptional regulation, highlighting the importance of chromatin context in determining the transcriptional output of PHE1-bound genes.

papers.title: Targeting the YAP1/TAZ-TEAD Transcriptional Axis Reveals a Therapeutic Vulnerability in Androgen Receptor Signaling Inhibitor (ARSI)-Resistant Prostate Cancer
papers.abstract: Therapeutic resistance remains a major barrier in advanced prostate cancer (PCa), particularly after prolonged treatment with second-generation androgen receptor signaling inhibitors (ARSIs) such as enzalutamide. Tumors can evade these drugs by escaping androgen receptor (AR) dependence through cellular plasticity and lineage transitions, but alternative resistance networks remain poorly understood. Enzalutamide-resistant (ENZ-R) PCa cells showed marked activation and nuclear enrichment of the YAP-1/TAZ-TEAD complex. Disrupting this transcriptional interface with CA3 shows strong anti-metastatic effects, inhibiting migration, invasion, and colony formation across AR-dependent and AR-independent PCa cell lines, suggesting efficacy regardless of cellular lineage or AR status. Similar effects with GNE-7883, K-975, and siRNA knockdown supported a class effect. In vivo, CA3 treatment substantially reduces tumor burden in PC3 and DU145 xenograft models, supporting the systemic efficacy of disrupting the YAP-1/TAZ-TEAD axis in aggressive, AR-independent disease. Mechanistically, this anti-tumor response is driven by potent cytotoxicity: CA3 induces substantial DNA damage and apoptosis in both in vitro and in vivo settings. Moreover, we identified increased YAP-1/WWTR1(Taz) expression as a negative predictor of therapeutic response in PCa patients. These findings indicate that enzalutamide resistance creates a targetable dependence on functional Hippo transcription. Small-molecule disruption of YAP-1/TAZ-TEAD may offer a rational strategy to counter treatment resistance and lineage escape in advanced PCa.

papers.title: TERRA engages MDA5 to shape the immune landscape in ALT brain tumors
papers.abstract: In cancer, telomere maintenance is mediated by telomerase reactivation or by the alternative lengthening of telomere (ALT) pathway. Both mechanisms contribute to cancer cell replicative immortality, but ALT, generates telomere instability and promotes inflammation, thus contributing to cancer progression also through non-cell autonomous mechanisms. How ALT telomeres modulate inflammatory signals in cancer is not fully understood, mostly because of the lack of organismal models of ALT+ cancers. Here we used a zebrafish model of ALT+ brain tumor to demonstrate that ALT telomeres promote inflammation through increased transcription of TERRA, which engages RNA-sensing pathways through MDA5. Analysis of ALT+ brain tumors shows that MDA5-MAVS signaling results in the production of interferon responsive genes and cytokines that induce a pro-tumoral immune microenvironment, which can be prevented by abrogating TERRA signaling through in vivo antisense technology, or by CRISPR/Cas9 mediated knock-out of MDA5 or MAVS. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis reveals that abrogating TERRA signaling using ASOs affects both cancer cells and immune cell compartments in a long-lasting manner. These findings reveal a previously unrecognized role of TERRA in modulating immune responses in ALT+ brain tumors and highlight the potential of TERRA-targeting ASOs as a novel therapeutic strategy for ALT tumors.

papers.title: Origin tracing and detection lag in the first Aedes albopictus invasion of mainland Australia and a long-term genomic dataset of mosquito incursions
papers.abstract: Proactive management of invasive species aims to prevent and eradicate new incursions before they establish. Genomic data can assist proactive management around how to deploy resources and when to change strategies, and has been used effectively in managing Aedes albopictus (Asian tiger mosquito) in the Australian Northern Peninsula Area over the past decade. This study characterises the first major incursion of Ae. albopictus on the Australian mainland, and contrasts this with long-term genomic monitoring of this species within the Torres Strait Islands (TSI). First, we genomically traced the mainland incursion, which was detected in Cape York, Queensland, to the nearest infested island, Muralug (Prince of Wales). Strong genetic drift patterns in the incursion are suggestive of recent inbreeding, and point to a lag between incursion and detection of at least two mosquito generations. This stands in stark contrast with incursions within the TSI, which showed no evidence of inbreeding, suggesting no detection lag in the TSI. We genomically traced n=63 incursions detected in the TSI between 2019-2026, including n=44 newly sequenced samples; this used an expanded reference databank containing samples from one island, Muralug, that had not been available in previous tracing. Including Muralug greatly improved tracing success from ~50% to 77.8-92.1%. We observed no reduction in tracing success when whole genome and reduced representation sequencing datasets were combined in analysis, indicating composite approaches are viable. Together these findings demonstrate the value of genomic databanks for long-term incursion monitoring, provided these capture a sufficient proportion of genetic variation.

papers.title: Autoinhibition and conformational activation regulate cell-wall anchoring of the bacterial type IV pilus machinery
papers.abstract: Type IV pili are widespread bacterial nanomachines that mediate adhesion, motility and host interactions, yet the molecular mechanism coordinating assembly of their outer-membrane channel with attachment to the bacterial cell wall has remained unknown. Here, we show that the conserved PilQ-associated protein TsaP functions as a conformationally regulated envelope adaptor linking secretin assembly to cell-wall anchoring. A crystal structure of full-length TsaP, integrated with structural, biophysical and functional analyses, reveals a compact autoinhibited conformation in which the N-terminal LysM domain is sequestered against the protein core. Comparative structural analyses support a mechanism in which PilQ association remodels TsaP, exposing the LysM domain for peptidoglycan binding. Together, our findings support a mechanistic model in which PilQ-dependent conformational activation of TsaP couples secretin assembly to cell-wall anchoring, providing a framework for understanding the regulated integration of type IV pilus machineries within the bacterial envelope.

papers.title: Detection of vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium and discrimination of vanA and vanB genotypes by VITEK MS Prime MALDI-TOF Mass Spectrometry and machine learning
papers.abstract: Rapid identification of vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium (VREfm) and discrimination of resistance mechanisms (VanA and VanB) are critical for appropriate antimicrobial therapy and infection control, particularly during outbreaks. Matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization-time of flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS), combined with machine learning, has emerged as a promising tool for this purpose. We evaluated whether MALDI-TOF mass spectra acquired on VITEK MS PRIME, combined with machine learning, could provide this information. Spectra from 388 from clinical and rectal surveillance samples (135 vancomycin-susceptible (VSEfm), 138 vanA and 115 vanB VREfm) were processed with Clover MSDAS, and four algorithms (partial least squares-discriminant analysis (PLS-DA), linear and polynomial support vector machines (SVM-L and SVM-P) and random forest (RF)) were trained to discriminate VSEfm from VREfm and VanA from VanB isolates. Model performance was evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation and using independent set of characterized E. faecium isolates from routine practice. Pairwise and triplet ensembles of these algorithms were also assessed. In the test set, PLS-DA was the best individual classifier for VSEfm versus VREfm (balanced accuracy, 78.9%), and the ensemble of PLS-DA and linear SVM reached 80.7%. Validation within routine isolates confirmed the models robustness, achieving 100% correct classification. Discrimination of VanA from VanB was more accurate: 93.2% with RF and up to 97.1% with ensembles. Identical sequence types were found among susceptible, VanA and VanB isolates, indicating that classification was not driven by clonal lineage. MALDI-TOF MS combined with machine learning is a promising, low-cost tool for VREfm screening and vanA/vanB differentiation.

papers.title: Centimeter-sized Human Vitreous Organoids from Pluripotent Stem Cells
papers.abstract: The vitreous, the largest intraocular tissue, provides a transparent light path and maintains the intraocular homeostasis. The reconstitution of the vitreous in vitro or in vivo remains an unsolved biomedical challenge. Here, we discovered a common feature, the "growth edge", constituted primarily of fibroblasts and their secreted proteins in human and mouse vitreous development. By leveraging the transforming growth factor beta signaling, we then generated centimeter-scale vitreous-like organoids (VOs) through stepwise differentiation from human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs). The VOs exhibited striking similarity to human vitreous in terms of physical transparency, vitreoretinal interface, molecular composition, biological profiles and regenerative transplantability. Lines of evidence supported that fibroblasts are the key cell hub for vitreous development. Finally, VOs with a transthyretin (TTR) mutation recapitulated the vitreous phenotypes of human patients with vitreous amyloidosis. Together, vitreous organoid technology opens avenues for future studies of human vitreous development, disease modeling, and regenerative therapeutics for a broad spectrum of human vitreoretinal diseases.

papers.title: Unraveling molecular mechanisms for specification of blastomere identity and neural fate in the annelid Capitella teleta
papers.abstract: The evolution of central nervous systems remains highly debated as we incorporate data on developmental mechanisms in understudied taxa. Yet how this process occurs in the third major bilaterian clade called Spiralia (e.g., annelids, mollusks) remains inconclusive. Using blastomere isolations, we previously found that in the annelids Capitella teleta and Platynereis dumerilii, ectodermal blastomeres fated to generate the brain and ventral nerve cord can form neural tissue after being isolated. However, in C. teleta, nerve cord formation can be inhibited or rescued by other blastomeres. To ascertain the molecular mechanisms underlying this process, we performed RNAseq on isolated blastomeres in C. teleta at the 8-, 16- and 32-cell stages and found differential expression of components of canonical Wnt signaling across the animal-vegetal axis when conditional neural specification is occurring. Furthermore, asymmetrical localization of TALE and FOX transcripts along the embryonic axis suggests a role in establishing blastomere identity, as observed in mollusks. Our data suggest the integration of an ancestral gene regulatory network of FOXQ2-cWnt and lineage-specific genes during early development, linked to the emergence of spiral cleavage.

papers.title: Membrane progesterone receptors spatially organize and partner with ABHD2 to mediate metabolic signaling
papers.abstract: Membrane progesterone receptors (mPRs) mediate rapid hormone responses, yet how they engage effectors remains poorly understood. Here, we reveal a spatially regulated partnership between mPRs and the lipid hydrolase ABHD2 that provides a mechanistic basis for the early steps of non-genomic progesterone signaling in mammalian cells. Agonist stimulation promotes mPR-dependent accumulation of predominantly intracellular ABHD2 at the plasma membrane and enhances its association with mPRs. Although human ABHD2 binds progesterone, its phospholipase A2 activity requires partnership with mPRs and an intact catalytic site. ABHD2 deletion disrupts agonist-induced metabolic signaling in hepatic and muscle cells and affects glucose homeostasis in obese mice. Together, these findings uncover a conserved receptor-hydrolase signaling mechanism in which spatially regulated association and receptor-dependent enzymatic activity emerge as defining features of non-genomic steroid signaling.

papers.title: The creatine transporter SLC6A8 is an immune pressure-exposed metabolic vulnerability in acute myeloid leukemia
papers.abstract: Chemotherapy imposes metabolic pressure that generates persisting tumor cell states, but whether these adaptations also shape immune evasion is poorly understood. Here, we identify creatine accumulation as a conserved feature of chemotherapy-persisting acute myeloid leukemia (AML) across mouse and human models. Stable-isotope tracing and genetic perturbation show that this is driven predominantly by SLC6A8-mediated creatine uptake rather than de novo synthesis. SLC6A8 was dispensable for AML proliferation and chemotherapy resistance but strongly promoted leukemia persistence under T cell pressure. This effect was independent of phosphocreatine generation and canonical energetic buffering. Instead, SLC6A8 deficiency increased cytokine-driven STAT1 signaling and chromatin remodeling, inducing the expression of antigen-presentation and co-stimulatory molecules, such as MHC-II, CD40, and CD80. Thus, creatine uptake via SLC6A8 is a non-canonical metabolic adaptation that restrains immune-driven remodeling and enables AML immune evasion. These findings link a therapy-induced metabolic adaptation to cytokine responsiveness and reveal SLC6A8 as a targetable vulnerability.

papers.title: The genetic basis of adaptation to continuous environmental gradients informs predictions about climate change responses
papers.abstract: A central goal of evolutionary genetics is to determine how environmental pressures maintain adaptive genetic variation, and evaluate how this variation is encoded in the genome. We leveraged two powerful approaches to identify genomic regions associated with climatic adaptation, test the genetic basis of climatic adaptation, and predict genomic responses to novel climates: genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of climate niche parameters derived from demographic models and genome-environment associations (GEA) of climatic factors with 2,737,409 loci. The GWAS found 319 unique single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) associated with climate niche parameters derived from demographic models using multi-year manipulative field experiments with Boechera stricta. The GEA detected 154 unique SNPs linked to climatic variation, with only one SNP found in both approaches. Local adaptation via adult survival arose primarily through conditional neutrality, as local alleles outperformed foreign alleles at only one end of the climatic gradient, rather than genetic trade-offs. Candidate genes near these loci were implicated in stress responses. Contrary to expectations, increasing temperatures and accelerating snowmelt timings did not augment the absolute fitness of low elevation genotypes. We found non-linear fitness functions for seedling recruitment at multiple SNPs detected via GWAS, with both conditional neutrality and genetic trade-offs evident in different portions of the climatic gradient. Local maladaptation arose exclusively in GEA SNPs. Our analyses revealed that the hot and dry conditions projected under climate change may rapidly exceed the tolerance of this species. However, we identified 47 SNPs at which evolutionary rescue or assisted migration could ameliorate the reduction in fitness under climate change.

papers.title: Comprehensive identification of bacterial and archaeal habitat associations using IndicPiper
papers.abstract: Taxa that are prevalent and abundant in a particular habitat more so than other habitats can be considered indicators of that habitat. In addition to providing basic natural history information, indicator taxa can be used to verify metadata assignments in large public databases, identify potential contamination, and assess contributions of different source populations to a sink population. Despite these potential applications, a comprehensive database of microbial indicator taxa for major habitats of interest does not yet exist. Here we present IndicPiper, a database and methodology that uses the Sandpiper database combined with indicator taxa analysis to identify the habitat associations of bacterial and archaeal genera. IndicPiper includes a clearly defined methodology and set of functions such that any user with a list of habitats of interest could run the functions and generate their own database. IndicPiper uses the Genome Taxonomy Database (GTDB) for taxonomy, and the provided database or custom databases can be used to analyze any prokaryotic sample-by-taxa abundance table, including those from shotgun metagenomic and 16S rRNA marker gene sequencing. After presenting the methodology and results, we then present three applications of IndicPiper on actual modern and ancient DNA sequencing datasets. We used IndicPiper to assess the contribution of different source habitats to Lake Tjornin sediments in Iceland over the past 2000 years, to paired indoor and outdoor dust samples from homes across the U.S, and to freshwater samples across the Willamette River watershed in Oregon, USA.

papers.title: A trade-off between desiccation resistance and social communication in a social bee
papers.abstract: The cuticular lipids of insects serve both as a barrier against desiccation and as chemical signals. In social insects, these lipids regulate reproduction and nestmate recognition, potentially creating a trade-off between waterproofing and communication. We tested this hypothesis in bumblebee workers by examining the roles of cuticular compounds in desiccation resistance and behavioral attraction. Desiccation survival varied with age, social state, and ovary activation, with fertile queenless workers showing the greatest resistance. Cuticular profiles changed markedly with age and social environment. Although the total amount of secretion remained similar among groups, queenright workers showed age-dependent decline in alkenes and a corresponding increase in two acetate esters (tetracosyl and hexacosyl acetate). To determine the functions of these compounds, we tested their effects on desiccation survival and attraction. Topical application of several hydrocarbons, but not tetracosyl acetate, increased desiccation resistance. In contrast, tetracosyl acetate, but not hydrocarbons, elicited attraction, and only in queenright workers. These results demonstrate an age-dependent shift in cuticular lipid composition in the presence of the queen from producing waterproofing hydrocarbons toward signaling compounds in the presence of the queen, reducing desiccation resistance while enhancing communication. Our findings suggest that the evolution of insect cuticular lipids has been shaped by both physiological demands and selection for complex social communication.

papers.title: Beyond the tripartite genome: a widespread, mobile and gene-rich accessory plasmidome expands the genomic landscape of the model symbiont Sinorhizobium meliloti
papers.abstract: Sinorhizobium meliloti is one of the best-studied nitrogen-fixing symbionts, yet research has focused almost entirely on its chromosome and two megaplasmids, pSymA and pSymB. Many strains carry additional accessory plasmids, but these large, pSymA-like elements are rarely recovered from short-read assemblies, leaving a hidden part of the genome unexplored. By sequencing 346 strains with long reads, we recovered 386 accessory plasmids from 76% of strains, with 318 absent from public databases, showing that accessory plasmids are the rule and not the exception. These plasmids were large (34-749 kb), including the largest accessory plasmid reported in S. meliloti, and most were mobilizable or conjugative (relaxases in 85% and mating-pair formation systems in 75% of plasmid clusters), equipping them to move between strains. RepA typing defined 13 replicon groups unique to Sinorhizobium, which could serve as a framework for tracking these plasmids in natural populations. We also found evidence of plasmid expansion by fusion, and one ~315 kb plasmid was a cointegrate of two smaller plasmids from our collection. About two-thirds of plasmid gene families were absent from the main replicons, including defense systems, the anti-restriction protein ArdC, and biosynthetic gene clusters, 53% of which had never been observed before. Overturning the view that S. meliloti lacks restriction-modification systems, we found them in 153 genomes, including on 32 accessory plasmids. Most inferred gene transfers stayed within the family Rhizobiaceae. Accessory plasmids thus form a large, mobile and largely unexplored gene pool that may shape how this model symbiont competes and adapts.

papers.title: Gene identity, not recoding strategy, determines the fitness cost of synonymous recoding in bacteriophage {Phi}X174
papers.abstract: Synthetic biology allows for the synthesis of genomes from scratch. Although technically achievable, our abilities in designing genomes that result in live organisms are in their infancy. One important consideration is synonymous codon usage bias, which is present in most organisms and shaped by selection for efficient translation. Many studies have edited the synonymous codon usage patterns of viruses with the goal of viral attenuation, but these studies almost always build a single construct per design, so we know little about how repeatable the effects of recoding are. We designed and built 111 synonymously recoded {Phi}X174 genomes, applying four recoding strategies at up to five levels of attenuation to each of three genes, with three independently designed replicates of most combinations. Which gene we recoded mattered considerably more than how we recoded it. Recoding genes for the major capsid protein F, the major spike protein G and the DNA pilot protein H in full, with the least-used synonym codons from E. coli cost 12.0, 10.8 and 5.9 doublings per hour, respectively. Recoding strategy per se had no detectable effect once the number of codons changed was accounted for. Predicted mRNA folding stability also had no measurable effect on fitness when tested in gene F, whose wildtype transcript is highly stable and could easily be destabilized with synonymous codon rearrangements. While the number of codons changed was correlated with the degree of attenuation, divergence between independently designed replicates increased as more codons were edited. Replicates of designs with small fitness effects varied little, while replicates of strongly attenuating designs diverged by several doublings per hour. The fitness outcome of large-scale genome recoding is therefore substantially unpredictable from the design variables alone: even among independently designed genomes receiving the same treatment, fitness can diverge substantially.

papers.title: Pharmacological CARD9 Inhibition Reduces Pneumocystis murina Burden In Vivo and Ex Vivo
papers.abstract: Caspase recruitment domain-containing protein 9 (CARD9) is an important adaptor protein of the innate immune responses to various fungal pathogens, including Pneumocystis species. CARD9 signaling is paramount in Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) host defense, and excessive inflammatory responses driven by this molecule can promote deleterious lung injury. We previously demonstrated that BRD5529, a first generation small-molecule CARD9 inhibitor, attenuates pulmonary inflammatory cytokine production during PCP. Here, we investigated the previously unreported effects of BRD5529 on Pneumocystis murina burden in vivo and in an ex vivo PCP-infected precision-cut lung slice (PCLS) model. In vitro, BRD5529 treatment (1 mg/kg) reduced lung organism burden in mice with established PCP, with an effect similar in magnitude to standard-of-care trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) therapy. In infected PCLS cultured with BRD5529 for 72 h, P. murina viability was also reduced, with the greatest reduction observed at lower BRD5529 concentrations. BRD5529 treatment did not reduce PCLS metabolic activity and viability after 72 h, as assessed by resazurin reduction. Together, these findings suggest that pharmacological CARD9 inhibition may impact organism burden/viability in addition to reducing lung inflammation during PCP.

papers.title: Linking Early Bacterial Responses to Growth Inhibition via Glucose-Turbidity Dynamics for Rapid Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing
papers.abstract: Earlier susceptibility information can guide timely antibiotic selection, while metabolic measurements can broaden the characterization of bacterial drug responses. We developed glucose-turbidity antimicrobial susceptibility testing (GT-AST) to pair residual-glucose assay signals with turbidity and relate early responses to growth inhibition. Among 43 cultured isolates, some antibiotic-exposed cultures showed glucose-associated changes despite attenuated turbidity responses. These observations provide physiological clues for studying metabolic activity when growth is limited, including future investigations of viable but non-culturable states or persister cells. Conventional broth microdilution relies on overnight growth readings; GT-AST used trajectories collected during approximately 2 h of antibiotic exposure to predict subsequent growth and estimate minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs). Across 100 repeats of isolate-grouped cross-validation, essential agreement between predicted MICs and independently measured reference MICs averaged 87.1%. Eight bronchoalveolar lavage fluid specimens were tested directly without prior bacterial isolation. Levofloxacin susceptibility classifications based on observed growth agreed with hospital results in all four culture-positive specimens. Exact and essential agreement between predicted and hospital MICs each averaged 99.0%. Together, these findings support developing GT-AST to provide earlier susceptibility information for effective, appropriately targeted treatment of patients. Keywords: antimicrobial susceptibility testing; glucose metabolism; turbidity; machine learning; minimum inhibitory concentration

papers.title: Candidate gene mining of a fragmented Tipularia discolor Pursh (Nutt.) genome assembly reveals genes putatively associated with specialized metabolite production.
papers.abstract: Orchids are a large and diverse group of plants with unique adaptations that have enabled the utilization of many different environmental habitats across almost all continents. These adaptations are mediated by an as-yet-underexplored genetic resource. Nearly all sequenced orchid genomes are of Asian origin and represent less than 0.1% of all orchid species, limiting the ability to explore and mine the gene space of this complex plant family. Greater representation of orchids in genome databases could provide important insights into the genes responsible for adaptive phenotypes, which could be useful for targeted crop improvement and in orchid conservation efforts. To begin to expand the palette of orchid genomes, an effort was undertaken to sequence the genome of a North American terrestrial orchid, Tipularia discolor. K-mer analysis estimated a haploid genome size of approximately 1.7 Gb, with a high proportion of repetitive sequences. Although a complete genome was not obtained, the implementation of a conservative gene mining approach and the generation of a candidate gene mining pipeline led to the identification of 68 consensus contig objects containing whole or partial genes related to sucrose, trehalose, terpenoid, and phenylpropanoid metabolism. Of note, two bibenzyl synthase homologs were identified with high confidence and clustered with characterized orchid bibenzyl synthases in a CHS/BBS phylogeny, indicating that T. discolor, like its Asian and South American relatives, has the capacity to produce this distinct class of phenylpropanoids. Thus, despite substantial fragmentation, the T. discolor assembly contains sufficient gene space representation for targeted candidate gene discovery. This works lays the foundation for functional characterization of selected candidates and development of a more complete genome assembly for comparative genomic studies.
